Title: Cisco chief found a 27-year-old ex-founder ‘buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic’—now he's upgrading 98% of its code | Fortune

URL Source: https://fortune.com/2026/10/30/cisco-president-jeetu-patel-gen-z-27-year-old-unlimited-ai-tokens-rewrite-legacy-code-entry-level-jobs/

Markdown Content:
Gen Z can’t catch a break. Entry-level jobs are[vanishing](https://fortune.com/2025/09/21/goodwill-ceo-preparing-for-influx-of-jobless-gen-z-ai-automation-kill-entry-level-jobs-youth-unemployment-crisis/);[some 40% of bosses](https://www.peoplemanagement.co.uk/article/1946118/employers-plan-reduce-graduate-hiring-ai-research-finds) say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for[showing up late](https://fortune.com/2023/11/15/mit-interviewer-gen-z-late-research-deadlines/) and refusing to put in[overtime for free](https://fortune.com/2024/04/29/gen-z-job-seeker-refused-90-minute-task-recruiter-slammed/). Cisco’s president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn’t buying it—he’s just handed one of the company’s biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart “five levels” below him.

“I’ve given him unlimited tokens because he’s going to refactor code,” Patel told _Fortune_ at a small roundtable dinner. “So I’m like, you can go, you can go nuts.”

The “him” is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or “Paddy,” as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant[acquired EzDubs](https://techcrunch.com/2025/11/17/cisco-acquires-translation-startup-ezdubs/), the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel’s words, “buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic.”

That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco’s San Francisco office, and the pair got talking. Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco’s legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren’t thinking that way.

So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of refactoring 98% of Cisco’s legacy code within 24 months.

Now, he’s on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will “challenge the system and the status quo,” or, as he puts it, be “an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up.”

## Cisco’s president says Gen Z should be teaching his veterans, not doing data entry—and he’s fine with the tension that causes

At most companies, only someone with decades of experience under their belt would be trusted with a project this size. Patel thinks that’s a problem.

“If you don’t hire the early-in-career [workers], and you just let your workforce continue the way that they were, where do fresh ideas get injected? How do you challenge the status quo?” he said.

Seasoned staff can still come up with new ideas, Patel added. What they can’t do is ask the questions that only someone with no experience would think to ask.

And getting the two to get along isn’t always smooth. Patel admits that putting a Gen Zer in a room with people who’ve been at Cisco for decades can create friction—but he says that’s the point.

“Tension is good,” he said. “I actually try to create tension in the teams because you want to have enough friction on the ideas. You don’t want to have friction with people and personalities.”

“What you have to do is establish enough trust with people to say you are going to be expected to create unreasonable goals for yourself,” he added. “And so, in order to go out and achieve those unreasonable goals, think outside of the box.”

And he’s not just pushing senior staff to take notes from twentysomethings. He said that he treats every intern as “kind of a reverse mentor,” and even does talks at colleges to find students who are “hungry.”

His latest Gen Z bet came out of one of those talks, to 17- and 18-year-old Stanford scholarship students. While a line of students fired questions at him, one, Baya, stood off to the side, just listening. She waited until everyone else had finished before she opened up.

He told her to email him every month with what she’d learned about AI. It was a test of follow-through: “Everyone can go out and have one good conversation. But are they going to stick with their commitments?”

She never missed one, landed an internship at Cisco, and redesigned “something” that experienced staff hadn’t been able to crack.

“I didn’t bring her in so that she can do grunt work and do data entry,” he said. “We brought her in so that she could actually teach our people how to think completely differently.” Now he wants to recruit her.

## Patel isn’t the only one betting on Gen Z—OpenAI investor Josh Kushner and Will.i.am are hunting for young, hungry talent

Patel isn’t the only boss who sees Gen Z’s lack of experience as an asset.

Thrive Capital’s founder Josh Kushner told _Fortune_ he specifically likes to[hire people with less than four years of industry experience.](https://fortune.com/2024/11/15/why-josh-kushner-the-lead-investor-in-openai-likes-to-hire-people-with-less-than-4-years-of-experience/?utm_source=search&utm_medium=suggested_search&utm_campaign=search_link_clicks)

When he launched the venture capital firm at just 26, he faced pressure to bring in older, more seasoned hires. But, as he put it, “anyone who has experience that is talented will never want to work with a 26-year-old.” So, instead, he recruited the “smartest people that we knew who were our ages.”

And that bet paid off: His firm made early investments in startups worth billions, including[OpenAI](https://fortune.com/2024/11/12/joshua-kushner-why-bet-on-open-ai/), which is currently raising up to $30 billion at a [$1.25 trillion valuation.](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/22/openai-funding-round-uae-investors.html)

These days, Kushner could easily hire industry veterans with glowing résumés—but he’d still rather “find that young, hungry person.”

Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise—a generative AI platform trusted by[PepsiCo](https://fortune.com/company/pepsico/), Nestlé, and Mars—is also actively looking for Gen Zers with zero experience.

“I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries or limitations in how they think about the world,” [Chen told _Fortune_](https://fortune.com/2026/04/06/while-other-ceos-freeze-entry-level-roles-this-ai-founder-is-hiring-gen-z-with-zero-experience/?utm_source=chatgpt.com). “They’re almost like AI natives themselves, having been born and raised in this new realm of opportunities. And I see some of the best ideas coming from the younger generation that have not yet been in the job market.”

And Will.i.am has reached a similar conclusion. The Grammy-winning Black Eyed Peas frontman might be best known for his chart-topping hits, but behind the scenes, he’s a serious investor too. He backed[Tesla](https://fortune.com/company/tesla/), OpenAI, and[Pinterest](https://fortune.com/company/pinterest/) before they became household names—and now, he’s betting on Gen Z for his next investment.

Why? He believes the next big tech breakthroughs will come from young innovators at MIT and Stanford. “They’re young kids, and they’re native to this,” Will.i.am[told](https://fortune.com/article/will-i-am-says-work-life-balance-for-people-working-on-someone-elses-dream/)_Fortune_. “So you want to hunt for that. That’s the only thing I’m focused on.”

And Patel told _Fortune_ that the trend toward hiring Gen Z will only continue, thanks to AI.

“The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we’re surrounded by people with a broad range of experience,” he said. “Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode.”

“Either of these groups by themselves aren’t nearly as potent as when all three work together. It’s what creates magic.”

Title: Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/helping-websites-express-ai-training-preferences

Markdown Content:
Today, we’re announcing that OpenAI will honor a common [signal⁠(opens in a new window)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-kelley-aipref-training-preference-signal/) in robots.txt, the file that lets websites express their preferences about the use of their content for foundational generative AI training. This voluntary effort makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.

Previously, website operators would identify individual crawlers and maintain separate rules for each and every provider. Having a shared signal across multiple providers reduces that work for operators.

We aim to implement the signal in the coming months, and will share another update with details about our implementation when we do so. This new signal will not replace the controls we already provide through robots.txt. Our existing [crawler controls⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots), which provide web publishers flexibility and control over their pages, will continue to apply and be respected.

This draws on the [ongoing work⁠(opens in a new window)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab/) of the Internet Engineering Task Force’s (IETF) AI Preferences working group. We’re joining other participants in the working group in today’s announcement of this shared signal, and believe this strengthens our continued participation in the IETF standards discussions. OpenAI will continue to adapt its practices as those conversations and the landscape continue to evolve in view of appropriate controls and fairness.

We believe this is a practical step toward an open web where people can publish and discover information, and website owners have clearer, simpler ways to communicate their choices about how their content is used. We encourage other AI providers to honor the signal.

articles.content:
Title: AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them.

URL Source: https://newsletter.signoz.io/p/ai-isnt-replacing-sres-its-deskilling

Published Time: 2026-02-28T13:45:17+00:00

Markdown Content:
> 💌_Hey there, it’s Elizabeth from SigNoz!_
>
>
> _This newsletter is_ a _n honest attempt to talk about all things - observability, OpenTelemetry, open-source and the engineering in between!
> &
> This piece took 6 days, 5 hours to be cooked, hope we served._🌚

There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days.

The first says **[SRE is the future of all software engineering](https://swizec.com/blog/the-future-of-software-engineering-is-sre/)**, that as AI writes more and more code, the humans who remain will be the ones keeping systems alive. The second says AI will devour every tech job alive, SREs included. Neither is particularly useful if you’re an SRE trying to figure out what your Tuesday will look like in 2027.

Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?

Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient.

Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉).

In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge published a paper called _**[Ironies of Automation](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Ironies-of-automation-Bainbridge/0713bb9d9b138e4e0a15406006de9b0cddf68e28)**_. It became one of the most cited papers in human factors research, and its core argument is almost uncomfortably relevant today.

Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for.

Ring any bells yet? 🙂

Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems.

The _exact_ problems that require deep _expertise_, the _exact expertise_ that atrophies when you stop practising.

Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing.

Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering.

Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today.

Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks.

PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model.

*   Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated.

*   Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation.

*   Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context.

But here’s the catch.

If _human_ SREs (okay, now we have to use adjectives like human 🥹) only engage with Tier 3 incidents, i.e. the novel, never-before-seen outages, where do they build the _intuition_ to handle them? Intuition is usually developed from years of hands-on incident response, pattern recognition built through repetition, and the kind of gut-level understanding of a system that only develops from painfully waking up at the odd hour to solve the bug that brought the system down.

This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture.

In medicine, a [recent study](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/langas/article/PIIS2468-1253(25)00133-5/abstract) found that endoscopists who used AI assistance for polyp detection saw their unassisted detection rates drop from 28% to 22% after a period of AI use. They got worse at the thing they were supposed to be experts in, not because they forgot the theory, but because they stopped exercising the skill.

In aviation, [research](https://flightsafety.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/IASS_2019_Behrend_Lafargue.pdf) has shown that long-haul pilots who rely heavily on autopilot systems experience measurable degradation in situational awareness and manual flying ability. The problem got serious enough that the FAA now mandates more manual flying time to counteract the effect.

Somewhere over the past year, AI stopped being a tool I occasionally reached for and became the first thing I reach for, _always_. My instinct now is to offload as much as possible and apply my own thinking only where it’s absolutely unavoidable. The problem is that these moments are becoming the only exercises my brain gets, and I can feel the _rust_.

We can draw a pattern here. The more you let the system handle, the worse you get at handling things yourself and here’s the truly dangerous part, _you don’t feel it happening_. It gets masked as hyper-productivity. Cognitive research suggests that because AI tools make tasks feel easier and enhance visible performance, users are often unable to accurately judge the true status of their own skills. You feel competent, dashboards look green, and then on a Wednesday, a novel incident hits that doesn’t match any pattern the AI has seen, and you realise the muscle has atrophied.

For SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated.

But there’s something even more concerning than deskilling, and researchers have started calling it _never-skilling_. Deskilling means you once had a capability but have since lost it. Never-skilling means you never developed it in the first place. For junior SREs entering the field today in an environment where AI handles most of the incident response workflow, the opportunities to build foundational intuition and muscle through hands-on practice are vanishing.

The training pipeline itself is broken and not _self-healing_.

SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult.

We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward.

A few approaches worth considering:

**Deliberate inefficiency.** Just as the FAA mandates manual flying time even when the autopilot is perfectly capable, SRE teams can designate certain incidents, even the ones the AI could handle, as _human-practice opportunities_. This can be considered as a long-term investment to keep skills fresh, although it might come at the cost of a super-fast solution

**Build for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side.** There’s a meaningful difference between a system where a human approves an AI’s recommendation and one where a human actively engages with the problem alongside AI. The former keeps humans in a supervisory role that Bainbridge (the lady who wrote _that_ research paper about 40 years ago) showed leads to vigilance decay, and the latter keeps them cognitively engaged.

Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture.

Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply.

We’re talking about SREs specifically because that’s the world we live in at **[SigNoz](https://signoz.io/)**. We build an open-source observability platform, the kind of tool that gives SREs the metrics, traces, and logs they need to understand their systems deeply. For us, this deskilling question is not a rhetorical fad; it directly shapes how we’re building AI into our product.

Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned.

One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would.

And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure.

The future of SRE is human _with_ AI intentionally designed to keep humans sharp, engaged, and ready for the 5% that really counts.

Here’s the**[LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/pranay01_something-ive-been-thinking-about-lately-activity-7428804029134225408-IXif?utm_source=social_share_send&utm_medium=member_desktop_web&rcm=ACoAAC3MkwYBDZBMgATtR9hOGisjheK_u1VDu6w)** our founder posted a few days ago, which inspired me to write this.

# Through Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart taught us the measure of a man

By[Jason Laughlin](https://www.bostonglobe.com/about/staff-list/staff/jason-laughlin/) and[John Hilliard](https://www.bostonglobe.com/about/staff-list/staff/john-hilliard/) Globe Staff,Updated October 29, 2026, 7:58 p.m.

Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. GLOBE PHOTO/ELLIOTT MARKS

[Patrick Stewart](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/29/metro/patrick-stewart-dies/?p1=Article_Inline_Text_Link) died yesterday, and for people of a certain age, a little bit of the future left with him.

For a certain, less-than-new generation of fans of Stewart’s 1990s television work on Star Trek: The Next Generation, there’s a sorrow that the man behind the larger-than-life Captain Jean-Luc Picard would be lost to a very real, very heartbreaking condition, Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia, according to his family.

Stewart, of course, was far more than Picard. He anchored the X-Men film franchise and was for decades a dynamo on stage. But there are reasons Captain Picard, commander of the Starship Enterprise, is the character he’s best known for. Over The Next Generation’s seven seasons, four movies, and a revival show —Star Trek: Picard — that ended just three years ago, he portrayed a model of what mature, responsible adulthood could look like for a generation of boys who were bookish, imaginitive, and maybe a little nerdy.

Title: Organization for Transformative Works Status

URL Source: https://www.otwstatus.org/

Markdown Content:
**Update** - Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been found so far. However, we want to make some things clear:
First, no AO3 data has been deleted. All your works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are safe.

Second, while we currently don't believe that the user database was stolen, we are also unable to rule it out. The AO3 database contains account information that may include your username, email address, IP address, and a hashed version of your password.

We use industry-standard techniques for storing passwords in a scrambled form that cannot easily be reversed. Even so, no hashing method can fully protect a weak or reused password from being cracked. As a precaution, we recommend that you change your passwords on any other sites where you use the same password as on AO3.

AO3 does not collect real names, so none could be exposed. Additionally, our donor information is held in an entirely separate system and is never linked to AO3, so that data has also not been exposed.

We will update everyone as our investigation continues; we may be unable to respond to individual inquiries from users. Please keep an eye on our official outlets for updates. Our next update will be posted when we have further information available.

Our current expectation is that AO3 will be down for a minimum of two weeks; however, it could take up to four weeks. During that time, we may be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state, meaning that not all features will be available and/or the site may be read-only. If we are able to do that, please be aware that we might have to bring the site back down unexpectedly as part of our recovery efforts. We will keep you in the loop for any developments.

Oct 30, 2026 - 01:27 UTC

**Update** - We estimate that service restoration for #AO3 will take around 2 weeks but it could be up to 4 weeks. We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved. Please stay tuned for further info.
Oct 29, 2026 - 17:41 UTC

**Identified** - AO3 maintenance is in progress. We expect it to take at least 12 hours, but it may take longer. We will provide updates as necessary.
Oct 29, 2026 - 09:03 UTC

**Investigating** - AO3 is down for maintenance.
